Vincent Pelote
Vincent Pelote is the Director of Operations at the Institute for Jazz Studies at Rutgers University. His early interest in jazz guitar led to a dual career as a jazz historian and music librarian.
Vincent was interviewed in Orlando, Florida on February 25, 2017 by Monk Rowe, Director of the Fillius Jazz Archive.
My name is Monk Rowe and we are in Orlando at the MLA conference, and I’m very happy to have Vincent Pelote with me today, Director of Operations at the Institute of Jazz Studies at Rutgers. Welcome.
Thank you, Monk.
You’ve been perking my ears up the last couple of days when I hear you talking to other people. And I can sense your passion for jazz and I’m going to start out with an easy question.
Thank you. I like easy questions.
How about defining swing for us?
[Laughs] Oh come on man. Please tell me you are joking.

No. I’m not. But it did occur to me that with the big band the last couple of nights, playing the tunes from that era, the 30s and stuff, that the solid rhythm underneath this [scats] those horn parts are so syncopated and that the wonderful, smooth sort of tension it creates is just astounding.

Yeah, exactly. And I like the fact that if you listen to those, the little figures that Fletcher Henderson or Horace Henderson did as backgrounds to the soloists, I think they are wonderful by themselves, just listening to those background figures. They’re very nice.
And they’re really tricky to play.
Yes. Exactly.
It made me appreciate the arrangers and the cats that played those things.
Sure.
Because sometimes you read about the fact that maybe they all weren’t great readers, but they, boy, they did that stuff so well.

Well and they also had section rehearsals I’m sure they sat down and the sections just rehearsed. I mean certainly that happened in Lunceford’s band a lot where the sections would just rehearse their parts and then when they came together, boom, they’re ready to roll. So exactly. They wanted to make sure they got it right and made it sound good.
Yeah. There was a — I was doing a little poking around about you.
Uh oh. © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-
It was all good.
Well good.
There was a magazine, you wrote, maybe it was a column, answers to your jazz history questions.
Oh no. Jazz Magazine out of Northport, New York. “Fragments” was the column.
Did you get — what kind of questions did people ask you?

All right. I was very young at the time, okay? In fact Chris White was the director at the time, so we are talking ’74, ’75. I was still in college, wet behind the ears just really sort of getting into the whole jazz thing. And the kind of questions that were sent were sort of like — I guess you call them trivia questions now you know. What recording did Rahsaan Roland Kirk play a sarrusophone on or some things like that. Also I will confess now that the magazine is defunct that some of those questions were plants. I asked my brother to ask me a question and I would put it in, or I would ask a friend to send me a question or ask me a question and I would include it. Because I didn’t want to just make up something. I figured so at least I could say legitimately that somebody asked me this, they at least sent it in. Because we had to have a column and sometimes nothing was coming in. We weren’t getting any people writing anything in. And I will admit there was one question that I wish to this day I could do over again, the answer. It was about Fletcher Henderson versus Benny Goodman. You know, why was Goodman successful playing the exact same arrangements that Fletcher Henderson played. And I was sort of into my — how can I put this — I was sort of into my black nationalist bag at that time, which believe me I’m nowhere a black nationalist in any way, shape or form, but at that time I was sort of sniffing around in that area. And of course I launched into this whole tirade about how well yes, the black musicians were treated like crap and Fletcher, his music was twenty times better than Benny Goodman’s, but because he was black — of course I didn’t know or was aware until much, much later was that Henderson was paid very well for those arrangements, he was paid probably better than most arrangers were getting at that time, and Goodman loved him. Goodman considered him like a second father, really. And really took him in when he disbanded his band in ’34 and put him basically on the payroll and just had him turn out charts for him. A lot of them he didn’t even use, he just put them in the library and never got back to performing them or recording them, but he gave the guy a steady gig. And then when their band disbanded later, when Fletcher re-formed and then disbanded later, Goodman took him back in the organization and that’s how he ends up on those Charlie Christian-Goodman things as the pianist, even though he had a perfectly good pianist in the band, Jess Stacy, who he didn’t use on any of those recordings. He gave them to Fletcher Henderson instead. I love the guy but his piano playing at that point was really very old fashioned, out of step. © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-
He wasn’t that effective a leader.

No. He wasn’t. Not at all. No. He just wasn’t. They talk about that accident that happened, the car accident, which after that he seemed very aloof and not really interested much in promoting the band very much. But even before that I kind of wonder how much of a leader he really was. I mean he didn’t have an Irving Mills like Ellington had or Cab Calloway, somebody like that. I mean Hammond sort of came in at some point and sort of tried to take the band, do stuff with the band and stuff, and get them recording sessions and I think did some English Columbia and things like that. But there was no person pushing the Henderson band like Mills and those cats were doing, and Glaser was doing for Armstrong. And I think that was the problem with that band you know. Fletcher just wasn’t a very good businessman. He just wasn’t.

Well a question — I don’t know if I would have had it back then — but I’ve never really been clear about Benny Goodman’s role with this integration thing and how that happened. And you had said something to me yesterday about it. And Helen Dance had talked about her role in that. But what’s your take on exactly how it happened.

Well my take on it is sort of what I’ve gotten from reading various books and articles. So I mean I wasn’t there so I can’t say I have any firsthand knowledge, but I just got the impression that, you know, he wanted these two musicians in his organization. He wanted Wilson and he wanted Hampton. But he was smart enough to know that if he put them in the full big band it was going to cause problems. Not that they weren’t going to cause problems anyway having them as a sideshow, but I think it caused less problems because they weren’t sitting in the band with the rest of the musicians and he could bring them out as a side act and then put them away when they were finished and that was fine. It seemed to be acceptable I guess, more so than if they were actually sitting in the band, in the section. I don’t know where Hampton would have sat because really there’s no place for a vibe in those arrangements, but certainly, I mean he carried two pianists. He had Stacy and he had Wilson. And I guess if he’d had his druthers he probably would have had Wilson on piano for the whole thing. But I’m just talking. I don’t really know for sure. But that’s how I kind of saw it. Like he wanted what he wanted but he did it in a smart way, I think better than what Artie Shaw did by sticking Eldridge in there and Cooper later with Eldridge sitting there in the section and the shit they had to put up with, I’m sorry, the crap they had to put up with. Yeah.
Well there sure are a lot of Benny Goodman stories.

Oh God I’ve heard them, tons of them. And I can’t figure it out, why he was like he was. I always tell people I think Terry Gibbs summed it up perfectly when he said, “The man was crazy. The man was meshuga.”
I bet today there would be a designated psychological definition for what he was about. © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-

Yeah. I’ll tell you who has probably very good insight, and you should talk to him if you haven’t already, is Loren Schoenberg at the Jazz Museum in Harlem. Because he worked with Benny for a number of years. And he got the full treatment, everything from praise to damnation, he got the whole thing. And Benny took his band away from him eventually. He took off his gloves man.
Touché. You know Joe Wilder, he went on that tour to Russia.
Oh.
Joe would not even say Benny’s name.
Yeah.
That clarinet player was all he would say. Just wow. For Joe Wilder, who was like a gentle man.

A nice man. I knew him. I used to meet him in New York with Ed Berger, we used to go see him play, and he would come and talk to me at the table. Always asked me about my brother. I thought it was so funny, he met my brother maybe twice and every time he saw me he asked me, “How’s your brother doing.” And I was so touched by that. And another musician who wouldn’t mention Benny because he had a run-in with Benny Goodman was George Duvivier. Like also I met him, and what he would do is he would always call Benny Carter Ben. He wouldn’t call him Benny. Because of the connection with Benny Goodman.

Wow. You know what I loved about Joe and I noticed it with Milt Hinton and other fellows of that generation is they were such gentlemen, they were so nice, but at the same time if you disrespected them, like in a business fashion or — I witnessed this like a couple of times. Someone suggesting that they weren’t living up to their obligations. They took the heat and they were wait a minute, don’t besmirch my professionalism. And it was really good to witness that. You can be a nice guy and also stand up for your —

I saw it with Benny Carter also. He played a club in New York, Carlos #1 I guess it was. It was a club that was on Sixth Avenue. And he insisted on being paid in cash. And the guy said he would, the owner of the club said he would. And the guy was going to go back on that after Benny had played. And Benny insisted, “You give me my cash, this is what we agreed on — you don’t give me my cash you know —.” I don’t know what the consequences would have been but it was quite obvious that he was making Benny very angry. And you don’t get Benny Carter angry. That’s a side of Benny you don’t want to see.
No kidding.

Yeah. All that stuff about him being a gentleman and all that stuff. Yeah, he is, but don’t rile him. Don’t mess with him. Really. He got his cash. Believe me. At the end of the night he got his cash. © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-
So I saw a video of you, I guess it was taken at the Association of Recorded Sound Collections.
Oh God.
And you were saying different people collect different things, and we all have our passions.
Sure.
So what was your passion as a young man.

My passion as a young man was always, like most kids I listened to the popular music of the day, I had my little transistor radio. Remember those little 9-volt transistor radios you used to put to your ear? Or you had the one earphone that stuck in. Yeah. So I had that and I generally listened to the black stations on the other end of the dial, you know, WWRL and I liked Motown and all that. But then my uncle, Lester Pelote, was a professional jazz guitarist in New York. He never really broke out of the local scene and eventually became a cab driver and that was pretty much it. But he used to come to the house a lot, in Jersey City, and visit his brother, my father. And I got interested in guitar at that point. And my father, who wasn’t a musician but who liked jazz and had really two jazz albums that he played consistently, especially when he was a little drunk, he played the Wes Montgomery Trio on the Riverside label, the first album that Wes ever made, and an album that Al Casey, they called “Buck Jumpin’ on Swingville Prestige. And he played those two records over and over and over again to the point where my sisters were complaining about it — stop it, dad. But you know I saw him listening to them and to me, as a budding guitarist, because I was interested in playing guitar because of my uncle so I was fussing around with it, I was listening to this and I said yea, I like Wes. Al Casey is more approachable. I can copy him better. Because it was mostly single note stuff and it was a simpler style, a simpler single string style, because he goes back to the 30s, and Wes was more of a post-bop guitarist, even though he started out playing Charlie Christian solos. And so his stuff was hard. And then the octave thing which was completely out of my — I didn’t know what the hell was even going on with that. And of course soloing in chords, using block chords was completely like — you know. So I fell in love with the Al Casey album first. But then I started listening to more and more Wes and he became my hero. And so my passion became that, and also again, I have to point to my sister’s collection. She had the record “Hello Dolly” in her 45 collection. Now I know it was a big hit in ’64, it knocked The Beatles off the chart that year, but I didn’t really dig the record until 1966, ’67, ’66. And I started playing it and listening to it and I liked it. I liked the other side better by the way, “A Lot of Living to do” was the other side of that record, the 45. But you know, I listened to it, and I knew about Armstrong, I knew he was supposed to be this great musician but by ’66, ’67, ’68, ’67, he was just © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-

appearing on shows and he had the handkerchief and he didn’t play much trumpet at that point and I was just kind of wondering what’s so great about this guy. I mean everybody thinks he’s so wonderful. Because “Hello Dolly” was nice but I didn’t see it as anything that really knocked me out. So I went to the local library in Jersey City, the Fine Arts Library, and I pulled out an album that had an old track of Armstrong playing “Big Butter and Egg Man From the West” with the Hot Five. And I listened to it and don’t ask me why, but as a kid I must have been 14 or 13, when he took that solo at the end of that record, after the vocal, I just perked. I just like wow, now I get it. I could see why this was great. Because I don’t think anybody else was playing like that. And I didn’t know that for a fact, because I wasn’t immersed in that time period of music, but something about it just sounded so modern and different than anything that preceded it. And the settings just seemed weird, that this archaic sounding recording had this great stuff coming out of it. And so I just started trying to find as much jazz from that time period as I could. And so, back to the Five Corners Library, pulling out more records, because you could take LPs out and you could take them home and play them and bring them back. And I had an old Wallensak open reel tape recorder, and I used to record the records after I got them and then I just played the Wallensak tapes back over and over and over again. And so my passion really became early jazz, circa 1920s, 30s, and up to the bop era. A little later I started getting into bop. But that’s how I did it. I went back to the beginning and I worked my way up to the modern jazz eventually. And you know I loved Bird when I finally heard Bird, and I didn’t find it all that radical when I heard him because I guess I’d been listening to stuff that, you know, post-bop, that was sort of in your head anyway. So I used to say I don’t know how swing people were so crazy, it sounded perfectly logical to me, what he was doing. But then I read that they weren’t happy with the bop stuff. They thought it was weird, and Chinese music Dizzy Gillespie called it, and all that stuff. But I didn’t get it. It sounded fine to me. But anyway, that was my passion. My passion was —
So you weren’t a moldy fig.
No I wasn’t a moldy fig at all. I loved bop and beyond.
It’s very curious how one thing leads to another, sometimes backwards.
Yeah.
I made the mistake of buying “Om” by John Coltrane when someone told me about John Coltrane. And it wasn’t the right record to get.
No.
And so it took me some time to even put another Coltrane record on.
Sure. Yep.
And so do you pursue this in higher education? How did this passion delve into a career? © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-

Okay, when I went to college — oh I played guitar all throughout high school, pretty much on my own. I mean I am a self-taught guitar player. I didn’t take lessons. And I just listened a lot, I got the Mel Bay books for guitar and I went through the whole chord system so I could have a system. I didn’t want just a bunch of chords, I wanted a system so that I could play whatever was put in front of me by just using this system. So I did that. Of course I’ve since learned I was playing these crazy chords, didn’t have to play with any — that’s another story. And I fell in love with the whole concept of playing in a rhythm section and just playing chords. To me that was the greatest thing in the world, that somebody would devote themselves to just doing that. Eddie Condon was my hero. I loved Eddie Condon for just sitting there and doing that, and Freddie Green of course. But there were other rhythm guitars. Everybody talks about Freddie Green, but there’s other ways to play rhythm guitar. His is not the only way. Marty Grosz makes that quite clear today, that there are other types of rhythm guitar that you can play. I mean Dick McDonough was that wonderful rhythm guitarist, as were, I can just rattle off a bunch of names. Clayton “Sunshine” Duerr, who played with Louie Prima and, or Mezz Mezzrow. He played with Mezz Mezzrow and his orchestra. So there’s a whole bunch of guys like that that were just great rhythm guitar players, without necessarily sounding like Freddie Green. So that became my passion. And so I went to college to be basically, I went to be a writer originally but I went on the wrong day. So there was no orientation day, so there was nobody from the English department there, but there was a guy from the music department, so I went over to him. His name was Chester Fanning Smith. He was a classical pianist.
And this was at what school?

This was Rutgers University in Newark. Yeah. So I went over there because I got accepted to Rutgers. So I figured okay fine, this is good, I will go to Rutgers and be an English major. But anyway he talked to me and he said, “You know there’s a lot of things you could do with a music degree.” And he was trying to talk to me about becoming part of the department. And he gave me this sheet of paper that had all the different types of jobs you could get if you got a music degree. And I was floored. Because I figured the only thing you could do with music is play, and I didn’t think I was good enough to be a performer. And so I looked at it and said, “Hey, not bad.” So I signed up to be a music major. And I told him, I said, “I really don’t know that much about classical music but I love jazz. I mean if you guys don’t mind me being a jazz guy, okay.” And he was like, “Sure, no problem, come on in.” You know. So I did it and I don’t know, all through the four years that I was there, four and a half years, I was in this constant fight where, you know, they were doing the classical thing. In fact I remember for my audition to be in, I guess the choir, they wanted you to sing a song, and so they were all singing these © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-
classical things. I chose “Moonlight Serenade.” That was my audition piece. Because I knew —
Not “Caro Mio Ben” right?

I taught this poor young lady to play piano behind me on this thing and I was terrible. I mean I am not a singer. I am horrible. And she put up with that. And today, we still talk about it today, sitting in the practice room, and she had to coach me into doing this. And another thing I did with the jazz thing is in the orchestration class we were given a little piece of music to orchestrate, and while they’re all doing classical things, I orchestrated a Duke Ellington thing. So every chance I got I tried to work that in, into my education, and it just never left me. It just stuck. So I settled on being a music ed teacher, because I figured all right, I would get out, I would probably get a stage band or a jazz band, a high school level thing, and I could do that. Because I didn’t want to be a vocal teacher. I didn’t want to do the vocal choir thing. I wanted to do a band thing. So I figured that’s going to be my thing. I was going to just be that. And maybe that’s where I’d be today if Ed Berger hadn’t called me and said, “Vinny, there’s a job at the Institute. We have a two year grant to catalogue sound recordings, and we need someone who knows something about jazz. We’ll teach you how to catalogue, but we just need the jazz expertise and I know you have it. Do you want to leave teaching and do this for two years.” I said, “Yes, take me away.” Because I’d been substitute teaching and it was like horrible, the kids were terrible, I couldn’t stand it anymore And I said, “I’ll take it. I’ll take it for two years and we’ll see what happens.” So I did. And it was the first time that anybody had done a catalogue project of that nature for jazz music on a national database. And that was OCLC at the time. That was the only national database that was really out there. So that’s how I got started. That’s really where the whole thing started. And I just never left. Because once the grant was out they applied for another one to do LPs. First it was 78s, then it was LPs, so I did that. And then after that we just sort of killed the whole thing and they realized, you know, Vinny knows more than just how to catalog sound recordings. He knows a lot about jazz. So they kept me on and just kept moving me from one thing to another.
Yeah. You were learning on the job.

Yeah exactly. And eventually I got a degree. I went down to New Brunswick’s library school and I got my degree in library science. And I was able to get the job that the librarian there had, before me. And in fact it was her — she in fact told me, “You should get the degree because I’m going to retire soon and you’ll probably be the perfect replacement, if you get your degree.” So I did. And I don’t recommend people get a degree just for one job. Because if I didn’t get that job I didn’t know what I would have done. Because I didn’t want to do anything else. I didn’t want to be a music librarian in © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-

some other institution. I wanted to be in the Institute of Jazz Studies. I mean if I didn’t get that job I don’t know what I would have done. But that’s weird. It just worked out. But it was a gamble. It was a big gamble.
Well I can attest that it’s a pretty cool place.
It’s wonderful. It’s always been.
What is the coolest thing in the collection, as far as you’re concerned?
As far as I’m concerned, oh God. There’s just so many things. I mean but I guess I’d have to say the coolest thing is Lester Young’s tenor saxophone.
That’s what I would have said. Because I was only there the one time but, oh look —

Yeah. There’s something magical about it. And I just look at it and I can see him holding it, that weird way he held the sax and everything, and those beautiful sounds coming out of that horn man. And I’m not even a horn player man, but I appreciate Prez man.
I love that moment that they captured on “The Sound of Jazz” with Lester and Billie.
And Billie. The face on her when he’s playing that solo. I mean she’s just like —
Just about a month ago I finally sat down and tried to write out his solo.
Oh cool.
You know, and compared to doing some transcriptions it’s not that hard. But it’s so perfect.

Yeah. It’s just amazing. I remember you showed the film when you asked somebody what do they think about when they improvise – I think it was Bill Charlap. And you know, his answer was actually perfect. I mean I guess you really don’t sit down thinking all right I’m going to go from a C7 now to, I’ve got to make the third go here. Because how can you? You can’t. Well you’re an improviser. You know. It’s just so ingrained in you, it’s like breathing I guess. And I guess that was Prez man. Beautiful music just came out of that horn, man. That’s great stuff. The other cool thing I would say, and this is because I am a guitarist, we have one of Eddie Condon’s guitars. It’s a four-string tenor guitar. And I just think that’s great, because I would have loved to have been in there when he was playing that thing.
I love reading about those guys. Like in Bill Crow’s book, you know.
He’s got great stories.

It’s the jazz life. And sometimes you wonder – well that’s another subject, about then and now. I cracked up at the rehearsal, I think it was last night, because one guy was going to say, he was saying, “we’re going to take a donation to collect a little money for some of the ringers.” So he says, “we’re taking a donation” and someone said, “do you take 78s?” I said, “How perfect is that?” What to do with the 78s.
Oh God we get that almost every day. So, but it’s, “Oh my father just died,” or, you know, “he had a collection of 78s.” Mostly it’s LPs that they want to give us. And you © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-

know, and they’re so convinced these are the most greatest most unique collection in the world, and, “Oh it’s got lots of Louis Armstrong and Duke Ellington and Count Basie.” And I hate to always tell them, “Yeah, these are probably kind of common LPs. We probably have every one of them that he had in his collection too, and we just can’t take them because we have no space.” The space is not there.
Has anybody ever used them?

Yes. People do come in and use it. And I was shocked one day when somebody came in, just one of the community people in the Newark community – because we’re open to everybody, we’re not just open to students, it’s open to everybody – he came in and he wanted to hear a Miles Davis recording. But he said, “I don’t want to hear the CD, I want to hear the LP.” And so I did a double take and said, “You sure? I mean it’s the same record.” “No, no, no” he said, “I want to hear the LP. The LP sounds different.” So I got him the LP and he was happy as a clam. But that’s so rare, really, that somebody is that insistent on listening to an LP. A lot of times we give people LPs because there are no CD equivalents. And that’s still, unfortunately, the truth. And I hate to hear about the impending death of the CD because not everything has been switched over. There are still LPs that you’ll never see on CDs. And that’s a shame, if CDs are going to die.
Oh right. They’re not going to make them anymore.
And downloading? I’m sorry. Maybe it’s just what pains me is the old fogy that I am, I do not like downloading. I just don’t. I don’t.
I agree.
I don’t care for it at all.
And I got a good deal of my jazz education from reading liner notes.
Yes, yes.
You know you’re in the record store and you’re reading and you learn who writes, who do you agree with, so I’m going to buy this because this person says this thing about it.

Yep. One of the first things I told Dan Morgenstern when I knew he was the Institute of Jazz Studies Director was, you know how many records I’ve bought strictly on the fact that you said it was a great record? And he gets all sheepish and everything.
Yeah, I was just going to say, “Well I hope you liked them.”
I said, “Dan, you’re the man.” You know.
Who are the most, I don’t know, short list of the most interesting people you’ve met doing your work?

Well I didn’t meet him, but I did some work for him, long distance work for him. I did some work on Leonard Feather’s book, Earwitness to an Era.” I think it was his last book. And he couldn’t come out to the Institute so he sort of hired me to do some digging and stuff. And he paid me nicely, gave me check and everything. And I knew of him, I © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-

knew about him from reading and all of that and I knew all of the great things he did in terms of promoting the music and everything. And so I was very happy and proud to work for Leonard Feather. As far as meeting other people, Gunther Schuller, I met Gunther Schuller who I thought was one of the nicest people ever. He was doing some work on his book about the Swing Era. He pulled out about a ton of LPs and sat down and listened to these things over and over and over again, which was great. And I really enjoyed him. And believe it or not I met him at the Institute, Bennett Lester Carter. Benny Carter. He came over, well, the Ed Berger connection. Ed’s father wrote the definitive biography of Benny Carter, and Ed wrote the discography. It was a two-volume thing. The first volume was the history of Benny, the biography. The discography was the second volume. And Ed did that whole thing. And it was wonderful. It was the second, I thought, comprehensive discography of an artist at that time, the first being Hendersonia, Walter C. Allen’s book, which is huge. But it’s a biodiscography of Fletcher Henderson that Walter C. Allen must have worked on forever. But it came out first, and then Benny’s book came out with Ed’s discography, which is just as comprehensive as anything Walter Allen did, maybe even more so in some ways. So when Benny came to the Institute, I even remember the first stupid question I asked him, I wish I could have taken that back, I said, “Well Benny,” you know, trying to show I know a little something about jazz, I think I might have called him Mr. Carter even, I wasn’t that comfortable with him yet. And I said you know, “Mr. Carter, could you sit down and tell me when the switchover from tuba and banjo, the switchover to bass and guitar. When did that happen exactly.” Like there was an exact date that this happened, some magical date. And he looked at me like I had three heads. But he was such a nice guy. He didn’t say what a stupid question. He just said, “Well,” he said, “some arrangements called for tuba and banjo and some arrangements called for bass and guitar.” And that pretty much was it.
No kidding.
There was no magical moment when this happened.
Right.
It just sort of evolved in time. And yeah I guess he was right.

I know. It’s like you want those things to have this — like when did music switch back to straight eighth notes. Well the day Chuck Berry — I mean you want this thing to be compartmentalized a little bit.
You do. And the other interesting person I meet there was also Walter “Gil” Fuller.
Gil Fuller.
